entries.meaning: Rama calls his friend's proposal a good means and says they should try it if fate assists. Lakshmana dislikes this counsel and is deeply pained by Rama's words: what trust can be placed in fate? The Lord should become angry and dry the sea. Fate is the one support of a cowardly mind, and only the idle cry, 'Fate, fate!' Rama smiles and tells him to be patient, assuring him that he will act accordingly. After calming his younger brother, Raghuraya goes near the sea, first bows his head in reverence, and then sits on a spread of darbha grass at the shore. After Vibhishana came to Rama, Ravana had sent agents behind him; disguised in monkey bodies, they observe every event and inwardly praise the Lord's virtues and his love for those who seek refuge.

The agents begin openly describing Rama's nature, so absorbed in love that they forget concealment. The monkeys then recognize the enemy spies, bind them all, and bring them to Sugriva. The monkey king orders their limbs broken before they are sent back. The monkeys bind them, parade them around the army on every side, and beat them in many ways; though the wretched agents cry out, they do not stop. The spies invoke the Lord of Kosala against anyone who takes their noses and ears. Hearing this, Lakshmana summons them, feels compassion, laughs, and has them released at once. He gives them a letter for Ravana and tells them to read the words of Rama's younger brother to the destroyer of his own lineage. They must also deliver his generous oral message to the fool: return Sita and meet Rama, or your doom has arrived.

The agents immediately bow their heads at Lakshmana's feet and leave, recounting the Lord's virtues. Singing Rama's fame, they reach Lanka and bow at Ravana's feet. Laughing, the ten-headed king asks Shuka for his own welfare, then sarcastically asks after Vibhishana, whose death has drawn very near: the fool abandoned rule over Lanka and will become an unfortunate worm in another's hand. He asks about the army of bears and monkeys driven there by cruel Time, whose lives the soft-hearted ocean has now protected, and again asks about the ascetics whose hearts greatly fear him. Did Shuka meet them, or did they turn back after merely hearing Ravana's fair fame? Why does he not speak of the enemy army's splendor and strength, and why is his mind so astonished?

Shuka asks his lord to accept exactly what he says, abandon anger, and listen graciously. The moment Ravana's younger brother met Rama, the Lord anointed him king. When the monkeys heard that the visitors were Ravana's agents, they bound them and inflicted many pains; they began cutting ears and noses but released them when the spies swore by Rama. As for Rama's army, even a hundred million mouths could not describe it: bears and monkeys of many colors are arrayed there, vast, terrifying, and fierce-faced. Yet the one who burned Lanka and killed Ravana's son has little strength compared with all the monkeys. There are innumerable named warriors, formidable and terrible, each with the vast power of countless elephants: Dvivida, Mayanda, Nila, Nala, Angada, Gada, Vikata, Dadhimukha, Kehari, Nisatha, Satha, and Jambavan, a mass of strength.

All these monkeys equal Sugriva, Shuka says, and no one could count the many millions like them. Through Rama's grace their strength is incomparable, and they reckon the three worlds as straw. He has heard that the army contains eighteen padmas of monkey troop leaders. There is no monkey in the host who could not defeat Ravana in battle. All grind their hands in supreme anger; they restrain themselves only because Raghunatha has not given the order. They could dry the sea together with its fish and serpents, or else fill it by heaping in vast mountains. They say they will crush the ten-headed king into dust. Roaring and threatening without natural fear, they seem ready to devour Lanka. The monkeys and bears are innately heroic, and Lord Rama stands over them; they can conquer even ten million Ravanas in battle.

Not even a hundred thousand Sheshas could sing the vastness of Rama's splendor, strength, and wisdom, Shuka continues. A single arrow can dry a hundred seas, yet Rama asked Vibhishana's policy and, merciful at heart, requests a path from the ocean. Ravana laughs: if this is the judgment of one who has made monkeys his allies, no wonder he accepts the firm words of a naturally timid counselor and persists in coaxing the sea. He tells Shuka not to praise falsely: he has fathomed the enemy's strength and intelligence, and what victory or glory can belong to one whose minister Vibhishana is fearful? Angered by the villain's words but mindful of the moment, Shuka takes out Lakshmana's letter and asks Ravana to have it read to cool his heart. Ravana takes it in his left hand and has a minister read. The letter warns him not to gratify his mind with empty words and destroy his lineage: opposition to Rama offers no escape even under the refuge of Vishnu, Brahma, or Shiva. He must either abandon pride and, like his younger brother, become a bee at the Lord's lotus feet, or become with his whole wicked lineage a moth in the fire of Rama's arrows.

Ravana listens with fear in his mind but a smile on his face, and mocks the letter publicly: its lowly ascetic author, fallen on the ground yet reaching for the sky, indulges in boastful speech. Shuka says every word is true and begs his lord to understand, abandon his proud nature and anger, and renounce hostility toward Rama. Raghubira's nature is exceedingly tender although he rules every world; if Ravana meets him, the Lord will show mercy and keep not one offense in his heart. Shuka asks only that Janaka's daughter be returned. When he counsels giving Vaidehi back, the villain kicks him. Shuka bows at Ravana's feet and goes where compassionate Raghunatha is; after telling his story, he receives his proper state through Rama's grace. Shiva explains that this wise sage had become a demon through Agastya's curse; repeatedly bowing at Rama's feet, the sage now returns to his hermitage. Three days pass while the dull ocean ignores Rama's entreaty, so Rama speaks in anger: without fear there is no affection.

entries.meaning: Rama asks Lakshmana to bring his bow and arrows so he can dry the ocean with a fire-arrow. A respectful request to a fool, affection for the crooked, a beautiful policy offered to the naturally miserly, a discourse on knowledge to one absorbed in possessiveness, dispassion described to the extremely greedy, and Hari's story told to an angry or lustful person are as fruitless as seed sown on barren soil. Raghupati strings his bow, to Lakshmana's delight, and fits a terrible arrow. A flame rises in the ocean's heart; crocodiles, serpents, fish, and other creatures panic, and when the sea knows they are burning, it abandons pride and comes in a Brahmin's form with a golden tray full of many jewels. A banana bears fruit only when cut, however much one waters it; hear, Garuda, a base person submits only when rebuked.

The frightened Ocean clasps the Lord's feet and asks forgiveness for every fault. Sky, wind, fire, water, and earth are by nature inert in their action; impelled by Rama, Maya produced them for creation, as all the scriptures sing. Each remains in the manner assigned by the Lord's command and thereby finds happiness. The Lord has done well to teach the Ocean; the boundary is also Rama's own creation. The Ocean then voices a hierarchical maxim that drums, the unlettered, Shudras, animals, and women are subjects of corrective discipline or handling. By the Lord's power the Ocean can become dry enough for the army to cross, but that would not be the Ocean's own greatness. The Vedas declare the Lord's command irresistible, and the Ocean will quickly do whatever pleases him. Hearing these very humble words, the compassionate Lord smiles and asks him to state a means by which the monkey army can cross.

words.grammar: verbal noun governed by के अधिकारी

entries.note: The gloss for ताड़ना is deliberately marked uncertain. In the immediate analogy it denotes corrective control or discipline applied to what the speaker calls naturally inert; later reception disputes whether it can bear a softer sense such as attentive handling. The line is the personified Ocean's speech, and this annotation retains rather than endorses its hierarchical wording.

entries.meaning: The Ocean explains that the monkey brothers Nila and Nala received a sage's blessing in childhood: heavy mountains touched by them will float through Rama's majesty. Holding the Lord's sovereignty in his heart, the Ocean will also help according to his strength. Rama should have the sea bridged in this way, so that the three worlds may sing this fair fame. The Ocean asks him to strike with his arrow the mass of wicked, sinful men who inhabit its northern shore. Hearing the Ocean's pain, merciful, battle-valiant Rama removes it at once. Seeing Rama's immense strength and prowess, the Ocean rejoices and becomes happy; after telling the Lord the whole matter, it bows at his feet and departs. The sea returns to its own abode, and this counsel pleases Raghupati. Tulsidas has sung this deed, a remover of the Kali age's stain, according to his understanding. The multitude of Raghupati's virtues is an abode of joy, a dispeller of doubt, and a destroyer of grief; O foolish mind, abandon every other hope and reliance and continually sing and hear it. Those who respectfully hear Raghunatha's all-auspicious praise cross the ocean of becoming without a boat.
